cards.text: This is the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite, and it's a burden against Nineveh, the same great city Jonah once warned (Jonah 3:3-4). Nahum doesn't warm up with small talk, friend. He goes STRAIGHT to who God is.
First line out of the gate: the LORD is a jealous and avenging God, full of wrath. He takes vengeance on His foes and reserves wrath for His enemies.

cards.question: Right after all that wrath, Nahum says the LORD is quick to anger.
The LORD is slow to anger and great in power, but Nahum says He will by no means leave the guilty ___.

cards.text: Then Nahum shows how big God's power is: His path is in the whirlwind and storm. Friend, I've got a gold base stuck to my feet and I STILL trip walking to the oven.

cards.question: If the LORD's path runs through the whirlwind and storm, what does Nahum say the clouds are?

cards.text: He rebukes the sea and dries it up, and Bashan and Carmel wither. Me? I rebuke my dough for not rising and it just sits there LOOKING at me.

cards.question: When the LORD shows up, what does Nahum say the mountains do?

cards.text: Then Nahum asks, 'Who can withstand His indignation? Who can endure His burning anger?'

cards.question: In Nahum's picture, God's wrath is poured out like fire, and even rocks are shattered before Him.

cards.text: Then, right in the middle of all that thunder, Nahum says the LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress. It's like the smoke alarm screaming and then somebody hands you a warm cookie.

cards.question: The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress. Who does Nahum say He cares for?

cards.text: Then Nahum says the LORD will make an end of Nineveh and pursue His enemies into darkness. Friend, I spent YEARS in the dark at the back of a junk drawer, and I do not recommend it.

cards.question: With an overwhelming ___, the LORD will make an end of Nineveh.

cards.text: Then Nahum says that whatever you plot against the LORD, He will bring to an end. You can plan all night long. He decides where it stops.

cards.question: Right after that, Nahum talks about affliction. He says it will rise up a second time.

cards.text: Then Nahum stacks up the pictures. They'll be tangled up as with thorns, and consumed like the drink of a drunkard.

cards.question: Nahum has one more picture. They'll be consumed like stubble that is fully ___.

cards.text: Then Nahum speaks right to the city. From you, O Nineveh, comes forth a plotter of evil against the LORD, a counselor of wickedness.
Now the LORD Himself speaks. And when the LORD says something, friend, you put the cookie DOWN and you listen.

cards.question: The LORD says that though they are allied and numerous, something will still happen to them. What?

answers.text: They will be cut down and pass away
They will be given more time
They will rule for many years

cards.question: Then the LORD turns to Judah. He says He has afflicted Judah, but He will afflict them no longer.
The LORD says He will now tear away Judah's shackles. What will He break from Judah's neck?

cards.text: Then the LORD issues a command concerning Nineveh. He will cut off the carved image and cast idol from the house of its gods.

cards.question: In that command, the LORD says Nineveh will have descendants to carry on its name.
No descendants and no idols. What does the LORD say He will prepare for Nineveh?

cards.text: Then Nahum says look to the mountains: here come the feet of someone bringing good news, proclaiming peace. I know that feeling, friend: the drawer slides open and the light pours in.

cards.question: Good news and peace are on the way. What does Nahum tell Judah to do?
Nahum tells Judah the wicked will never again march through them.

findings.problem: The setup 'Right after all that wrath' pushes the baker toward True. Nothing on the earlier cards lets a baker reason out that the LORD is slow to anger, so the right pick comes down to luck. The card also works against the baker instead of helping them reason.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: The blank is the last word of the line 'will by no means leave the guilty ___'. The baker has to guess the wording, not the meaning. 'Unnoticed' fits the meaning almost as well as 'unpunished'.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess a poetic detail: the clouds are 'the dust beneath His feet'. Nothing earlier lets the baker reason this out over 'a curtain around His throne' or 'a cloak on His shoulders'. It matches the Psalm 23 anointing-oil example the docs mark as bad.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The joke compares the LORD pursuing His enemies into darkness, which is judgment, to Papa Dorin being forgotten in the dark junk drawer. These aren't the same action. The comparison also loosely puts Papa Dorin among God's enemies and muddies the judgment in the verse.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: Judah shows up here for the first time and isn't introduced. Nothing says it's the southern kingdom of God's people. Without that, the baker doesn't know why the LORD turns from Nineveh to Judah.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."
